en: The Sūtra on the Four Matters Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, desiring to enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, Ānanda...
Nan addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that when devas, nāgas, spirits, ghosts, kings, and commoners met with the Buddha and heard his instructions and admonitions, there were none who did not rejoice."
According to their respective aspirations, some become śramaṇas and attain arhatship;
others remain householders, observe the five precepts, and upon death ascend to heaven.

Now that the Buddha has passed into extinction, upon whom shall the devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, the common people, and the fourfold assembly of disciples rely to obtain merit and attain deliverance?
"From whom shall we receive it next?
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Ānanda! You possess great compassion and empathy.
Among the various classes of devas and humans, there are none who have not attained liberation through you.

After my departure, the world will be known as the age of the five turbidities; the minds of people will be muddled and confused, naturally disordered by filth and defilement, and the world will abound in perversity, deprecating the good and exalting the evil—this is truly a cause for concern.
"Although this may be so in the world, I possess the scriptures and their earnest admonitions; if you follow them with all your heart, blessings will naturally accrue to you, so do not worry."

Although I have departed from this world, the scriptures remain; the Great Dharma of the Six Perfections does not accompany me in my passing. That practitioners attain deliverance is not through divine bestowal.
"Do you not understand what I have said? Ānanda then replied,
"I pray that you will explain it further."
The Buddha said:
"There are four great dharmas from which one may obtain merit and also attain the Way; the merit is exactly equal to that of attaining the body of a Buddha."
Ānanda spoke again:
"I pray that the Buddha will explain these four matters for me.
The World-Honored One said:

"One should nurture the young and the weak with a heart of loving-kindness. Upon seeing birds, beasts, insects, moths, or those of lowly status who depend on others for their livelihood, one should always feel compassion for them. According to what they eat, one should ensure they find relief; do not employ weapons or staffs to wound or take their lives. With a heart of deep sympathy and loving-kindness, one should be like a compassionate mother."

Whether they be devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, or common people, those who practice this loving-kindness shall obtain great merit, which is exactly equal to the merit of attending upon the Buddha’s own body.
This refers to one matter.

"When calamities and anomalies arise in the world, when floods and droughts are不调 (unregulated), when the five grains are not abundant, and when the people suffer from famine, lose peace in their native lands, and desire to rebel and flee;

when the king, ministers, and subjects possess ample stores of grain in their granaries—they should contemplate impermanence and realize that life and limb are difficult to preserve. They must not cherish their precious grain, but should know how to cherish the lives of others. They should give rise to a heart of compassion, distribute grain from the state granaries as loans, and provide relief to the destitute to sustain their lives, so that they may dwell peacefully in their native lands."
If the mind is stingy and greedy, and one is unwilling to practice giving, one should reflect with careful attention:
"When a person first comes into birth, the soul comes empty; it takes form as its own body by depending upon the vital energy of desire from its two parents."
Within the mother’s womb, one stays for ten months before being born; thus one may attain the joy of kinship and preserve one's life.
On days of sorrow and anger, the connection is severed; when exhaustion reaches its limit, life ends. Yet the soul does not perish; it seeks a body once again.
Nobility and poverty, honor and lowliness, all arise from past actions.

Regarding official rank, emoluments, kingdoms, and precious treasures, do not be deluded by them to the point of disturbing your noble virtue; for when one's life comes to its end, both the body and the treasures remain behind in this world and do not follow one along.

One should always maintain a compassionate mind and cultivate practice through the Way of the Sūtras. By means of the Buddha’s enlightened teachings, one should observe all people and things as being like illusions and transformations, like dreams and echoes; all are empty and cannot be maintained for long. To observe the world in this way is the ultimate truth.

The people of the world are deluded and confused; their minds dwell in perversion, deceiving and misleading themselves, much like one who buys brass for the price of gold. When the body dies and the spirit departs, they shall fall into the three miserable realms.

Reflecting thus with earnest attention, one should quickly practice giving, competing even with one's own life. To the poor, the beggars, the weak and aged, and the sick, one should give according to what is appropriate, lest their lives be cut short.
If one maintains such a state of mind, the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Bodhisattvas and great beings, and the devas, nāgas, and spirits will all take pity on them.

When their life comes to an end, wherever their spirit-soul is reborn, they shall immediately receive noble and honorable status; both body and mind will be at peace, calamities will not arise, and they will fully attain their supreme aspirations. This is no different from making offerings to the Buddha’s own person while he was in the world.
This refers to two matters.

"Within the kingdom there will be many thieves, water and fire disasters, calamitous anomalies, and sudden upheavals; poisonous vapors will spread and diseases will run rampant—all these are the deeds of dragon deities and ghost kings from the ocean. Thus, one contracts this poison, suffering from grave illness and distress."
These ghosts, spirits, and nāgas are all those who died from poison while hunting, slaughtering, or fishing with nets.

Their souls and spirits have either fallen into the sea to become nāgas or have been born through transformation as powerful great deities; they all know their past lives and, harboring resentment for old grudges, create mist and dew and exhale foul, poisonous vapors to rain down upon that kingdom.

At that time, among the people, some died from poisoning while others merely fell ill; there were even those who smeared filth upon one another—all of which resulted from the lack of benevolence practiced by worldly people, their wanton slaughter of living beings, and their mutual resentment toward one another.
Those who kill with their own hands die immediately from the poison;
those who rejoice in the act all suffer further affliction and illness.
Whether they smear [the meat] upon one another or do not smear it upon one another, this is entirely due to whether there was a portion shared or no portion shared among those who eat the flesh.
The person of keen hearing perceives that the sin of killing pursues one without ceasing; measuring oneself by others, one knows they are exactly equal and no different.

If one practices in this manner, following the Buddha’s broad path and practicing the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—merit will naturally accrue to one's person.
If those from a butcher’s household give you meat, be careful not to eat it.

One who does not eat it will remain unstained by defilement, even while dwelling in an evil age, amidst thieves, calamities, and the miasma of poison. Even though situated therein, such a person shall not be tainted.

If the sovereign and the people possess abundant wealth and overflowing granaries, yet the orphaned, the widowed, and the solitary lack sufficient food and clothing, or if they are afflicted by severe illness and have no means to sustain themselves, one should provide them with medicine, medicinal gruel, and restorative care so that they may recover and their lives not be cut short by untimely death.

One should clearly understand that this person’s past lives were marked by evil deeds, a lack of faith in the Triple Gem, and a turning away from truth toward falsehood—all brought about by stinginess and greed. Since the distinction between sin and merit is clear, one must be careful not to commit evil;
furthermore, one should cultivate a heart of compassion and instruct the ignorant with the teachings of the Buddha’s sutras, causing them to uphold the Way of the scriptures.

If one saves a single person, enabling them to recover from illness, showing them the path of goodness, and causing them to uphold the five precepts so that they remain pure for the rest of their life and attend upon the Buddha’s body—the merit of these two acts is exactly equal.
These are called the three matters.
"In the world there are those of lofty integrity, pure and free from desire; there are śramaṇas and brahmins who cherish the scriptures and whose every word accords with the law."
The sovereign, ministers, and subjects should maintain a mind of reverence and solemnity when approaching to receive instruction on the laws of conduct.

What these eminent gentlemen have set forth with their own mouths are all the bequeathed scriptures of the Buddhas; they cause people to abandon evil and pursue good, providing a kindness exceeding that of one's own kin by more than a hundredfold, ensuring that at the end of life one does not fall into the three miserable realms, and one should always approach them with a compassionate heart and reverent solemnity.
It would be better to pour molten copper into one's mouth or have one's tongue cut off with a sharp blade than to slander or defame this pure person;
it would be better to sever one's own hand than to inflict such pain upon them;
it would be better to slit one's own belly, extract one's heart, and burn it than to harbor anger toward this person.

Suppose a fool, upon encountering the Buddha’s scriptures and the Way, clearly understands what to abandon and what to pursue; he distances himself from the masses who are stubborn and ignorant, hastens toward the assembly of the wise, and studies and receives the sacred texts to achieve high virtue.
“Śramaṇas and brahmins do not engage in trade or seek profit, for these are defilements of the person; their minds are pure and their conduct is clean, like a bright moon-pearl.
They maintain their alms-bowls and labor with their bodies to beg for food, taking only what is necessary to sustain the mouth and storing no surplus.
Whether they dwell in monasteries, or stay in mountain marshes, under trees, or among burial mounds, they all know their past lives.”
Discerning the true from the false, he composed scriptures to serve as a bridge for the world;
with a compassionate heart and great pity, he sat and rose while reciting incantations and prayers for the emperors, ministers, and commoners, so that the nation might enjoy peace and stability.

A man of such high caliber instructs the gods, dragons, and spirits with his virtue, moving their hearts; because he does not concern himself with worldly affairs, he is free from the failings of sensual desire, and thus he is praised and extolled by all who behold him.

If there are wise people among the king’s ministers and subjects, they should seek out such a person and provide them with the necessary clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for illness to ensure their peace and security, so that they may preach the sutras and precepts, expound upon and instruct others, practice seated meditation and mindfulness, and thereby either attain the Way or ascend to heaven after death.

To provide clothing and food for the defiled and corrupt people of an entire nation is not as meritorious as providing wholehearted offerings to a single pure practitioner; the latter's merit is vast and great, equal to that of making offerings to the Buddha’s own body when the Buddha was in the world, without any difference.
These are the four matters.
"When emperors, kings, ministers, and subjects look upon such people as these, there are no devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits who do not protect them, assist them, and rejoice."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In my previous lives, I practiced these four matters, receiving blessings through successive rebirths until I attained Buddhahood myself.
For this reason, I have repeated the teaching on these four matters."
Ānanda! You should extensively expound this to the devas, kings, ministers, and subjects: the wholesome deeds one performs will bring their own blessings and shall never go to waste.
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; I entrust four matters to you.
Having heard this sutra, Ānanda was both sorrowful and joyful; he stepped forward and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet to pay him homage.
The Sūtra on the Four Matters Spoken by the Buddha to Ānanda
